name: Eyelash curler
lead: An eyelash curler is a hand-held clamp with a curved frame and a replaceable rubber or silicone pad that bends the upper lashes into a curl. Users apply it at the base of the lashes, often before mascara, to make the eyes look larger and more open; the curl is temporary and lasts a few hours.[1][12] Heated versions, which Grokipedia dates to the late 1990s, are used to help the curl last longer.[1][12]

The look it creates follows from simple geometry: lashes that sweep upward leave the whole eye and upper lid more visible, and curl is a trait that varies widely between people, so a curler lets someone with straight lashes borrow a shape they do not have naturally.[13] In looksmaxxing forums, male users discuss curling as a cheap way to open up the eye area and soften a heavy upper lid, and compare it with lash lifts, tints and mascara.[10][11]

Published literature on the tool is largely case reports of injury and allergy, plus one laboratory study that found lash curler use did not measurably change eyelash structure, unlike mascara frequency.[2][3][4][5][6][7]
infobox: $5-20; some forum users cite 2-3 euros in shops and about 30 euros at beauty retailers[10]
US patent April 7, 1931, original brand Rodal, later Kurlash, per Wikipedia;[12] Grokipedia gives an earlier 1925 patent to Charles W. Stickel[1]

paras: Standard curlers have two hinged handles, a curved upper bar and a pad that cushions the lashes. Mini versions exist for the lash corners and for small eyes, and heated curlers use a battery-powered element.[1] Wikipedia describes the traditional design as spring-loaded, clamping lashes between two metal plates with rubber pads, curved to match the natural shape of the eye, and notes that it is sometimes warmed with a hair dryer beforehand, though not enough to burn the delicate lid skin. Heated curlers produce a more intense, longer-lasting curl.[12] Shiseido and Shu Uemura are named as manufacturers, and the general design has stayed similar since the 1940s.[12]

Wikipedia says the eyelash curler was patented in the United States on April 7, 1931, under the original name Rodal, and that the brand later renamed the product Kurlash.[12] Grokipedia gives a different account, saying the first verifiable patent was granted to Charles W. Stickel of Rochester, New York, in 1925 and that the device was marketed as Kurlash; the two sources have not been reconciled here and Grokipedia is an AI-generated source.[1][12]

Lash curling sits within a long history of eye cosmetics. Wikipedia on mascara dates kohl to about 4000 BC in ancient Egypt, credits Eugene Rimmel with an early petroleum-jelly cosmetic in the 19th century, and traces Maybelline to Thomas Lyle Williams's mail-order business in 1917.[14] False lashes were patented by Karl Nessler in the UK around 1902 to 1903 and by Anna Taylor in the US in 1911, and a lash-perming method is linked to a 1905 hairdressing technique.[15][16]

Heated curlers followed in the late 1990s, and Japanese manufacturers have been influential in curler design, according to Grokipedia.[1] Lash perms, now called lash lifts, became widely available after 2000.[16]

The clamp bends lashes around the curve of the pad, and the shape holds because the keratin partly sets in its new position; heat is claimed to extend the curl.[1] Wikipedia on the eyelash notes that lash length is largely genetic, usually 7 to 8 mm on the upper lid, that curl varies widely within populations, and that follicles form before birth so the number of lashes cannot increase.[13]
Users and makeup guides describe a curled lash line as making eyes look wider. The curl is temporary and fades within hours. No trials of appearance effects were identified.[1]

A 2014 study using synchrotron X-ray tomography on lashes from 36 Japanese women found that mascara use frequency correlated with cuticle cracking and cortex porosity, while eyelash curler use did not alter lash structure to a statistically significant degree.[4]

Lash lifts use perming chemistry: lashes are fixed to a silicone pad or rod, a perm solution is left on for 10 to 15 minutes and then a neutraliser, softening the lash so that it sets around the pad; the process takes about 30 to 45 minutes and results last roughly two to three months.[16] Wikipedia says the FDA has not approved the procedure for use around the eyes.[16] Consumers on Mumsnet discuss at-home lash lift kits as a longer-lasting alternative to curling.[9]

Lash extensions attach individual lashes with semi-permanent glue, last three to four weeks and come in classic, volume and hybrid styles.[15] The 2009 FDA approval of bimatoprost (Latisse) for lash growth was reported to increase upper lash length by up to 25 percent.[13] An October 2025 optometry clinical report lists allergens from glues, lifts and tints among eye risks, noting that formaldehyde and ethyl cyanoacrylate in lash glues can cause redness, swelling and allergic eye inflammation, and that allergens from lifts and tints stay in the lashes until they are replaced, about three months.[8]

Case reports describe nickel-related contact dermatitis from metal curlers, reported in 1985 and 1991.[5][6][7] Open-globe eye injuries involving curlers have also been reported, including a 2009 case report and a 2025 report in a beautician.[2][3] Optometry commentary lists curlers among cosmetic eye tools that can cause injury.[8]

Wikipedia says pulling on lashes while curling can weaken the roots and that holding the clamp down for long periods can make lashes weak or shed; pulled lashes take about seven to eight weeks to regrow, and repeated pulling may cause permanent damage.[12][13] Clinicians' general cautions in these sources include avoiding pinching the lid, avoiding use on wet or heavily coated mascara that may pull lashes, and using heated tools carefully.

Lash curling is discussed on looksmax.org as a quick, cheap way to open the eye area for men with long natural lashes or a heavy upper lid, and sometimes as a fix for visible upper eyelid exposure.[10] One thread, titled as 'eyelash curler maxxing', argues that careful use is subtle enough that new acquaintances would not notice it.[11] Alternatives such as finger curling with a balm, lash lifts and curling mascara are compared in the same discussions.[10][9]

No trials of eyelash curlers for appearance were found. Human studies are limited to case reports of dermatitis and eye injury and one cross-sectional laboratory study of lash structure.[2][3][4][5][6][7]

lore.intro: Eyelash curlers are discussed on looksmax.org mainly by male users asking whether curling natural lashes can improve the appearance of the eye area, and whether the tool damages lashes [10][11].

claims.claim: Curling lashes gives a 'prettyboy' effect and can disguise a weak eye area
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user with long natural lashes says curling them with his fingers hides part of his upper eyelid exposure (UEE) and gives a 'prettyboy' effect, and asks where to buy a curler [10].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined whether lash curling changes perceived attractiveness or eye-area proportions; the clinical literature on curlers consists of injury and allergy case reports [2][3][5][6][7].

claims.claim: Curlers can cut or damage lashes, so finger-curling with Aquaphor is a better method
claims.believers: One reply in the thread says curlers can damage lashes and that he instead curls with his fingers after applying Aquaphor, though the curl lasts about two hours and needs repeating [10]. The original poster also asks whether curlers can cut lashes, citing complaints by TikTok users [10].
claims.experts: A synchrotron imaging study of lashes from 36 Japanese women found that mascara use frequency correlated with cuticle cracking and porosity; it did not test curlers [4]. No published studies have compared finger-curling or Aquaphor with curlers.

claims.claim: A pricier, better-designed curler works better than a cheap one
claims.believers: Thread participants note curlers cost 2-3 euros in many shops but around 30 euros at beauty retailers, and one asks whether more expensive models are better [10]. A second thread's author says one specific brand is 'the one to go for' [11].
claims.experts: No published comparisons of curler brands, price tiers or pad designs exist.

claims.claim: Curler use can be subtle enough that new acquaintances cannot tell, and is considered attractive
claims.believers: The author of a looksmax.org thread on 'eyelash curler maxxing' says that if used carefully, anyone who has not met him before probably would not be able to tell, and cites before-and-after images as examples of a look considered attractive [11].
claims.experts: No published research evaluates how observers perceive men's curled lashes. A 2025 optometry clinical report on cosmetic eye enhancements discusses the eye-health caveats of such products [8].

claims.claim: Curlers are safe as long as the user is careful not to overdo it
claims.believers: The same author says he will 'have to be careful not to overdo it' and does not describe injury as a concern [11].
claims.experts: Case reports describe an open globe injury from an eyelash curler [2][3], and contact dermatitis from nickel in curlers [5][6][7]. Optometry commentary lists curler-related eye injuries among the risks of cosmetic eye enhancements [8].

claims.claim: Lash lifts and tints give a longer-lasting version of the same look.
claims.believers: Consumers discuss home and salon lash lifts as a way to keep a curl for weeks rather than hours.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says lifts last about two to three months and that the FDA has not approved the procedure around the eyes, and an optometry report notes allergens from lifts and tints remain in the lashes until they are replaced.[8][16]
